newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian supply craft takes oxygen to Mir.
newsitem.headline: Russian supply craft takes oxygen to Mir.

text.p: A Russian Progress-34 cargo craft blasted off on Sunday with oxygen reserves and equipment to help the two Russian cosmonauts and a U.S. astronaut aboard the Mir space station repair their on-board air supply.
The unmanned craft blasted off on on schedule at 1604 GMT, a spokesman for mission control in the town of Korolyov near Moscow said by telephone.
"It is now in orbit already and preparing for docking," another mission control official said later.

Progress was carrying 50 kg (110 lb) of pure oxygen -- two weeks' supply -- for use in an emergency, the official said. There were also tools and parts for repairs to on-board oxygen-making equipment damaged by leaks to Mir's cooling system.
"There's no reason for concern about a shortage of oxygen on the Mir station," said the official.
"This problem will be resolved soon," he said, adding that there were enough oxygen balloons on board to last a month and that repairs would start as soon as Progress docked on Tuesday.
NASA officials said on Friday that the leaks had knocked out a device used to maintain breathable air on board.

They said backup systems were running and that repairs would start at the weekend but a senior NASA official said the U.S. space agency would nevertheless review safety on Mir before sending any more astronauts to live and work there.
Mir's current U.S. resident, Jerry Linenger, who has spent 82 days aboard the station, was to be replaced in mid-May by astronaut Michael Foale.
NASA officials said they hoped to get a new Russian-made oxygen generator aboard the shuttle Atlantis, which is bound for Mir on May 15.
NASA's shuttle-Mir programme director Frank Culbertson said the space station was showing its age but he was confident the Russians would keep it operating.
"Right now it looks very positive. Unless there were some other failures, there is almost no likelihood we would change our plans," he said.
The 11-year-old space station has been hit by a series of problems, including a brief but intense fire which broke during use of the back-up oxygen supply.
An official from the Russian Space Agency, which coordinates manned space flights, said there were also big problems getting fuel for the Soyuz booster carrying the Progress into space.
As well as the air supply equipment, Progress is carrying food, scientific equipment, laundry and cleaning materials as well as presents from the relatives of those on board.
